Agustín de Iturbide. The Mexican general and statesman who completed the independence war begun by Miguel Hidalgo, crowned himself emperor, and established Mexico as a sovereign nation. His reign was brief but transformative, bridging colonial and modern Mexico.

Iturbide initially fought for Spain against Hidalgo's rebels, but he switched sides and unified the independent factions under the Plan of Iguala in 1821. That plan was a masterpiece of political compromise. It promised independence, monarchy, and religious unity, which united both conservatives and liberals around a common cause. In 1822, Iturbide crowned himself Emperor Agustín I, making Mexico an empire rather than a republic. His empire lasted only two years. He was forced to abdicate in 1823 as republicans rejected the very idea of monarchy. Exiled to Europe, he attempted to return to Mexico in 1824, but he was captured and executed by firing squad in Tamaulipas. Despite his brief reign, he secured Mexican independence and established the nation's first government. He shares the achievement of independence with Miguel Hidalgo, whose rebellion he brought to victorious conclusion, and his reign established the government that led to the later republic that Benito Juárez would embody.
